name: Petrified Wood
spiritual: Supports reflection on past lives and lineage
physical: Traditionally linked to endurance and stability
Associated with a feeling of being rooted
Often kept nearby for comfort when feeling unsettled
summary: Petrified Wood is ancient wood turned to stone, a grounding talisman for endurance, ancestry and perspective, often 200 million years old.
intro: Petrified wood is the fossilized remains of trees in which the original wood has been slowly replaced by silica minerals such as quartz, chalcedony and opal. The conversion is so detailed that growth rings, bark and even cell structure can still be seen in the stone. Colors depend on trace minerals: iron gives red, brown and yellow, manganese produces pink and black, and copper can create greens and blues. Polished slabs look like wood turned to jewelry. Large logs and fragments are found in dry badlands around the world, and the stone is cut into bookends, cabochons, spheres, tables and tumbled pieces.
history: People have collected petrified wood for thousands of years, often wondering at trees made of stone. Famous sites include Petrified Forest National Park in Arizona, which preserves trees that grew about 225 million years ago in the Triassic, and the Petrified Forest of Lesbos in Greece. The wood in such places was buried quickly by volcanic ash or sediment, then replaced molecule by molecule as mineral-rich water flowed through. Native American groups used pieces for tools and ornaments, and settlers built houses and fireplaces from it. Today, collecting from public lands is restricted in many areas, so be sure the piece you buy came from a legal source.
meaning: Petrified wood is the stone of ancestry and endurance in the crystal tradition. Healers link it to the root and earth star chakras and use it to feel rooted in family history and the long story of life on Earth. It is said to help people who feel unsteady during change by offering the patience of something that took millions of years to form. Many use it to reflect on lineage, heritage and the memory of those who came before. It is also linked with stability, discipline and the idea that long-term effort can turn something soft into something lasting. People also use it in grief work as a reminder that what matters can last in a new form.
howToUse: Place a piece of petrified wood on a desk, shelf or altar as a symbol of endurance and heritage. Hold a polished slice during meditation, tracing the growth rings with your fingers. Carry a small tumbled stone for grounding on stressful days. Use a slab as a base for candles or ancestor altars. Wear a pendant or cabochon for steady contact. Combine it with smoky quartz or black tourmaline for deeper rooting and protection.
care: Petrified wood is hard and generally water safe. Rinse it under lukewarm water, brush off dirt and dry with a soft cloth. Cleanse by smoke, sound, moonlight, burying in soil or on selenite. It tolerates sun and moon. Pieces with cracks or partial replacement can be fragile, so avoid soaking, knocks and sudden temperature changes. Store it apart from harder gems, and keep large slabs on a stable surface.
identify: Real petrified wood shows wood grain, growth rings or bark texture, with a stony, cool and heavy feel. Imitations can be made of resin, cast stone or painted rock with printed rings. Look for natural cracks, uneven color and three-dimensional grain that continues through the piece. Opalized wood is more colorful and sometimes translucent. Ask where the specimen was collected, as laws protect some sites.

faq.q: How does wood turn to stone?
faq.a: Buried wood is slowly replaced by silica-rich groundwater, molecule by molecule, until the original organic material is gone and the shape remains in quartz or opal. The process can take millions of years and preserves fine details like growth rings.

faq.q: What is petrified wood used for in crystal practice?
faq.a: It is used for grounding, patience and connection to ancestors. Crystal healers link it to the root and earth star chakras and keep it on altars or desks as a symbol of endurance.

faq.q: Is it legal to collect petrified wood?
faq.a: Rules vary. Collecting is banned in national parks like Petrified Forest in Arizona, and limited on many public lands. Buying from a reputable dealer who sources from private land or permitted areas is the safest choice.
